segments.caption: Day 3 of 100 Days of Machine Learning: the machine learning workflow.
The 7 steps every real project follows, one example from start to finish, and the mistake most beginners make. Save this one!
Everyone thinks machine learning is about choosing the perfect algorithm.
In real jobs, training the model is maybe 10% of the work. The other 90%? Everything around it.
Let's build one project, step by step: predicting flat prices in Pune.
Step 1: define the problem.
What exactly do we predict? The price of a flat, in lakhs. That's a number, so it's a regression problem.
And how will we judge success? Say, our predictions should be within 5 lakh on average.
Step 2: collect data.
We gather past sales: area, bedrooms, location, age of the building, and the price each flat actually sold for. Say, 10,000 flats.
Step 3, the biggest one: clean the data.
Real data is messy. Some rows have missing prices. Some flats are listed twice. Someone typed the area as 12,000 instead of 1,200.
We fill or remove the gaps, delete duplicates and fix the typos. Garbage in, garbage out.
Step 4: explore the data.
We plot it and look for patterns. Bigger flats cost more. Flats near the IT parks cost more. Older buildings cost a little less.
Step 5, the one beginners skip: split the data.
We hide 20% of the flats away. The model learns from the other 80% only.
Why? It's like an exam. If you've already seen the question paper, a high score proves nothing.
Step 6: train the model.
On the 8,000 training flats, the model guesses, measures its error, and adjusts, again and again, exactly like we saw on Day 1.
Step 7: evaluate, then deploy.
Now the exam: the 2,000 hidden flats. The model's predictions are off by 4 lakh on average. Our target was 5. Passed!
So we put it in an app, and keep watching it. Prices change, so the model is retrained every few months.
So remember the 7 steps: define, collect, clean, explore, split, train, evaluate and deploy.
Save this. It's the map for the next 97 days.
Your turn: a model scores 99%, but it was tested on the same data it trained on. What's the problem? Vote in the caption poll!
